blockers.quote: Day twenty: misconception first. You sign a binding purchase agreement on a flat with a view, half a million's worth, payable on day thirty-one, nothing leaving the account, sure that doubling grows slowly enough to leave you with just enough for this one.
blockers.why: On day twenty, the balance is already $524,288 (2^19), which already exceeds the half-million-dollar flat. Believing that eleven further doublings will grow 'slowly enough to leave you with just enough' for half a million is a straw man; Wagenaar and Sagaria (c05) demonstrates intuitive underestimation of exponential growth from a base, not believing that doubling an already-held $524k eleven times yields $500k.
blockers.fix: Stage the wrong belief earlier in the ladder (e.g., around day ten or fifteen, where extrapolating doubling to day thirty-one intuitively feels like it will only yield half a million), or frame day twenty's wrong belief as expecting day thirty-one to reach only a few million rather than over a billion dollars ($1,073,741,824).

blockers.quote: | c | EVERYTHING. | C | Scale: a person at a pier kiosk holding more than the whole world makes in a year |
blockers.why: The thumbnail image across all three variants (line 93) displays day thirty-one's balance of 1,073,741,824 ($1.07 billion). Claiming this image shows 'a person at a pier kiosk holding more than the whole world makes in a year' contradicts c01, which establishes world output at about $128 trillion (a threshold not passed until day forty-eight at $140.7 trillion).
blockers.fix: Revise the promise description for pair C/c to clarify that the thumbnail visual depicts day thirty-one ($1.07 billion) while Title C promises what the story later delivers at day forty-eight, or reject variant c in favor of recommended pair A/a ('DAY 31.').

keep.quote: Whatever is in your bank account at midnight is doubled by morning, starting from the one-dollar coin your grandmother sends you on your birthday, and it will not stop: in a month it buys the pier you live on, by day forty-eight it is bigger than everything the whole world makes in a year (about $128 trillion, the IMF's 2026 projection; claims.md c01), and by day fifty-eight it overflows the number box most computers count in (c06).
Most money, sir, is made when a bank lends. And when a loan is repaid, the money doesn't go anywhere. It stops existing. The Bank of England wrote that down in 2014.
"On most computer systems, the number box is sixty-four bits. And because the bank counts in cents, day fifty-eight overflows into a negative nineteen-digit number (c06)."
